a: only not with an undivided heart
p: Kings says Amaziah was good but 'not like David'. Chronicles puts it inwardly: his heart was not whole.
b: Kings measures Amaziah against David and Joash (2 Kings 14:3). Chronicles keeps the praise but replaces the comparison with levav shalem, "a whole, complete heart," the phrase David used of Solomon (1 Chronicles 28:9; 1 Chronicles 29:19) and that the site renders "undivided heart" in 2 Kings 20:3. The phrase sets up the chapter: Amaziah obeys the prophet once (25:10), then brings home Edom's gods (25:14). A half-loyal heart, in Chronicles' telling, shows itself in time.
orig: בְּלֵבָב שָׁלֵם (belevav shalem), 'with a whole heart'

a: Fathers must not die because of their children
p: Chronicles quotes the same law as Kings, but with 'die' where Kings and Deuteronomy have 'be put to death'.
b: The law reads, "Fathers must not be put to death because of their children" (Deuteronomy 24:16). Kings quotes it with the same passive verb, at least in its first two clauses (2 Kings 14:6). Chronicles has the simple verb yamutu, "they will die," three times. The change is tiny in writing (the same five letters with the w moved: ymwtw for ywmtw). It also has a foothold in Kings itself: the written text (Ketiv) of the last verb in 2 Kings 14:6 is yamut, "he will die," where the margin reads yumat, "he will be put to death." Either way the wording moves the law from a rule for courts toward a principle about how God deals with people, the principle Ezekiel 18:20 and Jeremiah 31:29–30 announce. It fits Chronicles' habit of judging each generation for its own deeds.

a: three hundred thousand picked men
p: Chronicles often gives Judah's army huge totals. Readers explain them in several ways.
b: Amaziah's 300,000 is modest beside Asa's 580,000 (14:8) and Jehoshaphat's 1,160,000 (17:14–18), and Uzziah will have 307,500 (26:13). Such totals are far beyond what archaeologists estimate for Judah's whole population in the 700s BC, perhaps 100,000 to 120,000 people. Some readers take the figures at face value. Others think 'elef, "thousand," once meant a military unit or a clan's contingent, so that "three hundred 'elef" was three hundred units. Many critical scholars think the numbers are symbolic, showing the strength God gave faithful kings. The same note applies to the numbers in 28:6 and 28:8.

a: The LORD is not with Israel, nor with any son of Ephraim
p: The man of God says the LORD is not with the northern army. Chronicles faults the northern kingdom, not northerners.
b: Chronicles treats the northern kingdom, founded in rebellion against David's house and the temple (13:5–12), as outside God's blessing, and so its soldiers can bring no help. Yet the same book calls northerners "brothers" (11:4; 28:11), has a northern prophet rescue Judean captives (28:9–15), and has Hezekiah invite Ephraim and Manasseh to Passover (30:1). The line drawn here is about the kingdom and its army, not the people. In Chronicles "Israel" can mean the north, all twelve tribes, or Judah as the faithful remnant (see 28:19).

a: It is in the LORD's power to give you far beyond this
p: Amaziah worries about a hundred talents already paid. The prophet tells him to write it off.
b: A hundred talents of silver was roughly three and a half tons. The prophet does not offer a refund; he tells the king that obedience will cost him, and that God can make up the loss. Jewish and Christian teachers have used the verse as a lesson on giving up gain for faithfulness (compare Mark 10:29–30). Critical readers note how it fits Chronicles' pattern: kings who rely on foreign help (here northern mercenaries) are rebuked, as Asa was for paying Aram (16:7–9).

a: They brought them to the top of the Rock
p: Kings says Amaziah captured Sela. Chronicles has captives thrown from 'the Rock', hassela, the same word.
b: 2 Kings 14:7 says Amaziah "seized Sela in battle" and renamed it. Chronicles does not mention the capture, but its "Rock" (hassela') is the same Hebrew word, so the two accounts likely recall the same place: a cliff-top stronghold in Edom, once identified with Petra and now often sought near Bozrah (see the note on 2 Kings 14:7). Throwing prisoners from a height was a known war atrocity. The prophets condemn other war atrocities when foreign nations commit them (Amos 1:11–13; Amos 2:1), and Chronicles reports this one without comment.

a: from Samaria to Beth-horon
p: The dismissed troops raid Judah. The route 'from Samaria' is odd, since Samaria lay in Israel.
b: The angry mercenaries strike while Amaziah is away fighting Edom. Beth-horon guarded the western road up to Jerusalem, on the border of Benjamin. "From Samaria" probably means they set out from the northern capital and struck south as far as Beth-horon, since Judah's towns did not reach Samaria. Some commentators suggest a copying error for another place name, but no manuscript supports one. The raid explains why Amaziah later challenges Israel (25:17).

a: he brought the gods of the people of Seir with him
p: Ancient armies carried off the images of defeated gods. Amaziah does that, and then worships them.
b: Assyrian and Babylonian kings regularly carried off the statues of conquered peoples' gods as trophies, and sometimes returned them as a favor. The Philistines did the same with the ark (1 Samuel 5:1–2), and Isaiah mocks Babylon's gods carried away on animals (Isaiah 46:1–2). Amaziah's sin is not the capture but what follows: he stands the images up and bows to them. The prophet's question in 25:15 exposes the absurdity: these gods had just failed to protect their own people.

a: Is it the king's counselor we have made you?
p: The Hebrew root ya'ats, 'counsel', runs through the scene: counselor, God's counsel, my counsel, took counsel.
b: The king silences the prophet with a sneer: did we make you a royal yo'ets, "counselor"? The prophet answers with the same root: God has "counseled" (ya'ats) to destroy you, because you would not hear my "counsel" ('etsah). The next verse says Amaziah "took counsel" (vayyiwwa'ats) and challenged Israel. The writer lets the word carry the verdict: the king rejected the right counsel and took the wrong one. The Plain English keeps "counsel" each time so the play can be heard.
orig: הַלְיוֹעֵץ לַמֶּלֶךְ (halyo'ets lammelekh), 'a counselor to the king?'

a: Joash son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel
p: Kings mostly calls this northern king Jehoash. Chronicles' Hebrew uses the short form Joash throughout.
b: The two forms, Yo'ash and Yeho'ash, are the same name, "the LORD has given." In 2 Kings 14:8–16 the northern king is usually Jehoash, and the site prints that. Chronicles' Hebrew has Joash every time, so this page prints Joash, as it prints Amaziah's father Joash. The site's policy is to keep each verse's own Hebrew form rather than smooth the names out. The fable and challenge in 25:17–24 copy 2 Kings 14:8–14 almost word for word; see the notes there.

a: It came from God, so that he could hand them over
p: Kings says only that Amaziah did not listen. Chronicles adds that God was at work in his refusal.
b: Chronicles adds the same kind of comment when Rehoboam refuses advice (10:15, from 1 Kings 12:15) and when Ahaziah goes to meet Jehu (22:7). The point is not that Amaziah was forced, since the prophet had already given him the choice (25:16), but that God turned his pride into his punishment, "because they had sought the gods of Edom." Jewish and Christian readers compare Pharaoh's hardened heart (Exodus 9:12) and Ahab's lying spirit (1 Kings 22:20–23). Critical scholars see Chronicles' doctrine that sin is punished within the sinner's own reign.

a: son of Joash son of Jehoahaz
p: Kings calls Amaziah's grandfather Ahaziah. Chronicles calls him Jehoahaz, the same name with its parts reversed.
b: 2 Kings 14:13 has "son of Jehoash son of Ahaziah." Chronicles has "son of Joash son of Jehoahaz." Ahazyahu ("the LORD has grasped") and Yeho'ahaz ("the LORD grasps") use the same two elements in reverse order. Chronicles already called this king Jehoahaz once (2 Chronicles 21:17) and Ahaziah elsewhere (22:1). Swapping the divine element from back to front is a known pattern in Hebrew names, like Jehoiachin and Jeconiah.

a: He brought him to Jerusalem
t: He came, or he brought him?
p: Kings' margin and Plain say Joash 'came' to Jerusalem. Chronicles agrees with Kings' written text: 'brought him'.
b: In 2 Kings 14:13 the written text (Ketiv) has vayvi'ehu, "he brought him," and the margin (Qere) vayyavo, "he came"; the site's 2 Kings Plain follows the margin. Chronicles has "he brought him" with no variant, so it stands as an early witness to the written text of Kings. The captive king is led into his own city before its wall is broken.

a: in Obed-edom's care
p: Only Chronicles names the keeper of the temple treasures. Obed-edom's family were gatekeepers over the storehouses.
b: In 1 Chronicles 26:15 the lot for the south gate fell to Obed-edom, "and to his sons the storehouse." Chronicles assumes the family still kept the temple stores in Amaziah's day, about two centuries later, so it names them as the ones from whose care the gold and silver were taken. The ark had once stayed in an Obed-edom's house and brought blessing (1 Chronicles 13:14); now the treasures in his family's care are carried to Samaria.

a: From the time Amaziah turned away from following the LORD
p: Kings reports the plot against Amaziah with no reason. Chronicles ties it to his turning from God.
b: In Kings the conspiracy simply happens. Chronicles adds, "From the time Amaziah turned away from following the LORD," linking the plot to his worship of Edom's gods. Taken strictly, the plot brewed for years, since Amaziah lived fifteen years after Joash (25:25). Readers in the traditional view take the line as the writer's insight into cause and effect. Critical scholars see Chronicles' method: a disaster in Kings is given a cause in the king's own sin, so that each reign shows its own reward or punishment.

a: the city of Judah
p: Kings says Amaziah was buried in the City of David. Chronicles' Hebrew says 'the city of Judah', a name for Jerusalem.
b: Most of Chronicles' burial notices have "the City of David." Here the Hebrew has 'ir Yehudah, "the city of Judah," which the Greek and some ancient versions change back to "City of David" (see the variant). The phrase is not a slip in sense, though: the Babylonian Chronicle calls Jerusalem "the city of Judah" (al Iahudu) when it reports Nebuchadnezzar's capture of it in 597 BC. Chronicles may preserve an old way of naming the capital.

a: Uzziah
p: Kings mostly calls this king Azariah, 'the LORD has helped'. Chronicles calls him Uzziah, 'the LORD is my strength'.
b: The same king appears as Azariah in 2 Kings 14:21–15:7 and 1 Chronicles 3:12, and as Uzziah in 2 Kings 15:13–34, Isaiah, Hosea, Amos and Zechariah. Chronicles uses Uzziah throughout this chapter, and the site keeps each verse's own form (see the note on 2 Kings 14:21). The two names may be a birth name and a throne name, or two forms of one name, since the roots 'zr (help) and 'zz (strength) were close in sound. Chronicles plays on both: God "helped" him (26:7), his army was "to help the king" (26:13), help came to him "until he was strong" (26:15), and "once he was strong" he fell (26:16).
orig: עֻזִּיָּהוּ ('Uzziyyahu), 'the LORD is my strength'; עֲזַרְיָה ('Azaryah), 'the LORD has helped'

a: after the king had lain down with his ancestors
p: Chronicles copies Kings' note about Elath before Uzziah's reign is even introduced.
b: 2 Kings 14:22 sets this notice right after Uzziah's accession, before his regnal formula in 15:1–2, and Chronicles keeps it in the same odd position. "The king" who lay down is Amaziah: Uzziah recovered the Red Sea port only after his father's death, perhaps a hint that Amaziah's last years overlapped with his son's rule. Kings spells the town Elath (2 Kings 14:22); Chronicles has Eloth, as at 2 Chronicles 8:17, and the site prints each book's own form. It is the same port, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba.

a: Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod
p: Uzziah broke the walls of three Philistine cities. Jabneh later became Yavneh, where the rabbis rebuilt Judaism.
b: Gath, near the border, had been taken by Hazael of Aram a generation earlier (2 Kings 12:17). Ashdod lay on the coast; Jabneh (Jabneel in Joshua 15:11) stood between them. At Gath (Tell es-Safi) the great destruction is Hazael's, about 830 BC; Aren Maeir's team has also found damage from an 8th-century earthquake, which they connect with the one dated to Uzziah's reign in Amos 1:1. Jabneh, later Yavneh or Jamnia, became the seat of the rabbinic academy after the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70. Amos, prophesying in Uzziah's day, still names Gath and Ashdod among Philistine cities (Amos 1:8; Amos 6:2).

a: the Meunites
p: A people of the desert south of Judah. The Greek calls them Minaeans, a South Arabian trading people.
b: Meunites appear again in 1 Chronicles 4:41 and among temple servants after the exile (Ezra 2:50). Many scholars link them to the Mu'unaya named in an inscription of Tiglath-pileser III, a desert people near Egypt's border, which fits Uzziah's push south toward "the way into Egypt" (26:8). The Greek translators read "Minaeans," the incense traders of South Arabia, here and in 26:8, where the Hebrew has Ammonites (see the variant). Gur-baal is unknown; for it the Greek has ἐπὶ τῆς πέτρας, "on the rock."

a: for he was a man who loved farmland
p: Uzziah built towers and cisterns for herds and farms. Royal estates are known from seals and jar handles.
b: The towers and cisterns in the wilderness and the Negev served herds and farms. Surveys have found many Iron Age forts and cisterns in the Judean desert and Negev, though dating them to one king is not possible. Two seals of royal officials name "Uzziyau" (Uzziah) as their master: "Belonging to Abiyau, servant of Uzziyau" and "Belonging to Shebanyau, servant of Uzziyau." Their authenticity has been accepted by most specialists. "Carmel" here is a common noun, "garden land," not the mountain. The note "he loved the soil" is unique among Chronicles' kings.

a: machines, inventions of an inventor
p: The Hebrew says 'devices devised by a deviser'. Many read catapults; others think of defensive screens on the walls.
b: The phrase chishvonot machashevet choshev repeats one root three times: clever things cleverly made. Older readers saw stone-throwing catapults. Catapults are first reported at Syracuse about 399 BC, and torsion engines only around 350 BC, so many critical scholars think the writer pictured the war machines of his own later day. Others note the Lachish reliefs of Sennacherib, which show Judean defenders behind frames of shields set on the battlements, and suggest Uzziah built such screens, from which archers shot and stones were dropped. Either way the point is the next line: his help was wonderful, until he was strong.

a: his heart rose up high, and it brought him to ruin
p: 'His heart was high' is Chronicles' phrase for the pride that comes after success. Hezekiah will fall into it too.
b: Gavah libbo, "his heart was high," names the danger of strength. Moses warned that a king's heart must not rise above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:20), and Proverbs says, before a fall comes a high spirit (Proverbs 16:18). Chronicles uses the same phrase for Hezekiah after his recovery (32:25–26), but Hezekiah humbled himself and Uzziah did not. "Brought him to ruin" (lehashchit) can also be read "he acted corruptly," as the KJV has it.

a: He went into the LORD's temple to burn incense on the altar of incense
p: David and Solomon offered sacrifices without blame. Uzziah is struck for burning incense. What was the difference?
b: Kings in the ancient Near East often served as priests, and David and Solomon led sacrifices (2 Samuel 6:17; 1 Kings 8:62–64). But the inner work of the sanctuary, burning incense on the gold altar inside the temple hall, belonged to Aaron's line alone (Exodus 30:7–8). The Law had warned that no outsider "was to come near to burn incense before the LORD, or he would become like Korah and his band" (Numbers 16:40). Jewish tradition reads Uzziah as wanting to be both king and high priest, and links his stroke to the earthquake of Amos 1:1 (Josephus, Antiquities 9.222–227). Christian readers note that Hebrews gives the joined office of king and priest only to Christ, after the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 7:1–3; Hebrews 7:14). Critical scholars see the writer's priestly concern for the temple's holiness.
r: Exodus 30:7–8; Numbers 16:40; Numbers 18:7; 1 Samuel 13:9–14; 2 Samuel 6:17; 1 Kings 8:62–64; Hebrews 7:1–3

a: Azariah the priest
p: The priest who stops the king is named Azariah, the name Kings uses for the king himself.
b: Chronicles never calls the king Azariah, and gives the name instead to the chief priest who stands in his way, with eighty brave priests behind him. Whether or not the writer meant it, readers of both books meet one Azariah confronting another. The priest's courage contrasts with the priests who failed under Ahaz (2 Kings 16:10–16) and recalls Jehoiada, who stood up to Athaliah (23:1–15).

a: the skin disease shone out on his forehead
p: The disease 'rose' on his forehead, where the high priest wore the gold plate reading 'Holy to the LORD'.
b: Tsara'at is a scaly skin disease, not Hansen's disease (see the note on 2 Kings 15:5). The verb zarach is used of the sun rising: it "dawned" on his face in front of the priests. The forehead matters. The high priest wore a gold plate on his forehead engraved "Holy to the LORD" (Exodus 28:36–38). The king who tried to do the high priest's work is marked on the same spot, and as one unclean he must leave the holy place at once (Leviticus 13:45–46). Miriam was struck the same way after challenging Moses (Numbers 12:10).
orig: וְהַצָּרַעַת זָרְחָה (vehatstsara'at zarechah), 'the skin disease shone out'

a: for he was cut off from the LORD's house
p: Kings tells of the 'house set apart'. Chronicles adds why: an unclean king could not enter the LORD's house.
b: The Law sent a person with tsara'at to live alone outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46). For a king this meant losing the temple and public life, so Jotham governed as regent (see the notes on 2 Kings 15:5). Nigzar, "cut off," is used of the dead in Isaiah 53:8 and Psalm 88:5, a strong word. Uzziah, who forced his way into the temple, ends his life barred from it.

a: the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz wrote down
p: Chronicles cites a work by Isaiah on Uzziah's reign. No such book survives; Isaiah's call came in the year Uzziah died.
b: Instead of Kings' royal records, Chronicles names prophets as the authors of its sources (compare 9:29; 12:15; 32:32). Isaiah received his call "in the year King Uzziah died" (Isaiah 6:1), so he was at least a young contemporary. The book of Isaiah contains no account of Uzziah's reign, so either Chronicles knew a work now lost, or it credits prophets with the history of their times as a way of saying the record is trustworthy. Traditional readers take the first view; many critical scholars the second.

a: in the kings' burial field
p: A stone plaque found in 1931 reads: 'Here were brought the bones of Uzziah king of Judah. Do not open.'
b: Kings says Azariah was buried "in the City of David." Chronicles adds a distinction: in a field belonging to the kings, not in the royal tombs, "for they said, 'He has a skin disease.'" In 1931 E. L. Sukenik published a stone plaque found in a collection on the Mount of Olives, inscribed in Aramaic: "Here were brought the bones of Uzziah king of Judah. Do not open." Its script dates to the first century BC or AD, so it marks a reburial, perhaps when Jerusalem expanded in the Second Temple period. It is now in the Israel Museum. It shows that Jews of that time still honored a known grave of Uzziah.

a: only he did not go into the LORD's temple
t: Not like his father in one thing
p: Kings' 'only' clause is about high places. Chronicles' 'only' is that Jotham did not repeat Uzziah's trespass.
b: 2 Kings 15:34–35 praises Jotham, then adds, "Only, the high places were not removed." Chronicles keeps the word "only" (raq) but changes what follows: Jotham did all his father did, except enter the LORD's temple, as Uzziah had done in 26:16. Some read "go into the temple" as meaning he did not even worship there, but in context it is praise: he kept the line his father crossed. The fault now lies with the people, who "still went on acting corruptly," preparing for Ahaz.
orig: רַק לֹא־בָא אֶל־הֵיכַל יְהוָה (raq lo-va el-heikhal YHWH)

a: the wall of the Ophel
p: The Ophel is the rise between the City of David and the temple mount. Several kings strengthened its wall.
b: 'Ofel means a swelling or bulge, the high ground north of the old City of David and south of the temple. Manasseh also built there (33:14), and the Ophel is named again in Nehemiah 3:26–27. Excavations south of the temple mount have uncovered Iron Age walls and buildings, some dated to the 800s–700s BC, though linking a stretch of wall to one king is uncertain. Jotham's building fits Chronicles' rule that faithful kings build and fortify.

a: ten thousand cors of wheat
p: A large tribute for three years. Ammon may have paid Judah while Assyria was busy elsewhere.
b: A cor (Hebrew kor) held perhaps 220 liters (about 6 bushels), so the grain alone would feed a sizable army. A hundred talents of silver was about three and a half tons. Ammon east of the Jordan had paid Uzziah too (26:8). The three-year limit may mean Ammon stopped paying when Aram and Israel pressed Judah in the 730s (2 Kings 15:37), or when Assyria took over the region. Chronicles alone records the campaign.

a: because he kept his ways steady before the LORD his God
p: Jotham is one of the few kings Chronicles praises without any fault. His strength is explained by his faithfulness.
b: Chronicles names a cause for everything: Jotham "grew strong" (vayyitchazzeq) because he set his ways in order before God. Kings mentions Rezin and Pekah beginning to harass Judah in Jotham's time (2 Kings 15:37), which would be a blot; Chronicles leaves it out and saves the attack for Ahaz (28:5). Critical scholars see the writer shaping events to fit his teaching; traditional readers see a selection that suits the book's purpose without denying Kings.

a: He walked in the ways of the kings of Israel
t: Ahaz, a northern king in Judah
p: Ahaz is one of the very few kings of Judah given no good word. Chronicles makes him a mirror of the northern kings.
b: Kings says Ahaz "walked in the road of the kings of Israel" and "even made his son pass through the fire" (2 Kings 16:3); Chronicles has the plural, "ways." Chronicles extends the charge: cast images of Baals (28:2), many high places (28:25), even shutting the temple doors (28:24). In 28:19 the Hebrew even calls him "Ahaz king of Israel" (see the variant). For Chronicles, Judah's king has become what the north was, and later in this same chapter a northern prophet and northern leaders act more faithfully than he does (28:9–15).

a: he burned his sons in the fire
p: Kings says Ahaz 'made his son pass through the fire'. Chronicles says 'burned his sons'. The Greek follows Kings.
b: The Hebrew of Kings has he'evir ba'esh, "made pass through the fire"; Chronicles has vayyav'er ba'esh, "burned in the fire," and plural sons. The two verbs differ by a single letter in Hebrew, and the Greek of Chronicles reads "made pass through," so some think a copyist's slip; others think Chronicles meant to say plainly what the older phrase meant. Whether such rites were always actual sacrifice is debated (see the topic). Ahaz's son Hezekiah survived to reign, so if real, the sacrifice was of another son.

a: So the LORD his God gave him into the hand of Aram's king
p: Kings says Aram and Israel besieged Jerusalem and failed. Chronicles tells only of Judah's heavy defeats.
b: About 734 BC Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel attacked Judah, apparently to force it into their alliance against Assyria (2 Kings 16:5; Isaiah 7:1–9). Kings says they hemmed Ahaz in at Jerusalem but "were not able to win the fight" (2 Kings 16:5). Chronicles reports two separate defeats with huge losses and mass captivity, and never mentions the siege or Isaiah's sign of Immanuel. The figure of 120,000 killed in a day (28:6) is far beyond what Judah could field, and many scholars read such numbers as a writer's way of showing scale. Assyrian records confirm the war's end: Tiglath-pileser took Damascus in 732 BC.

a: Oded
p: Oded is a prophet of the north, known only from this story, who stops Israel from enslaving Judah.
b: Chronicles mostly ignores the northern kingdom, but here it gives the north a faithful prophet and leaders who obey him. An earlier Oded was father of the prophet Azariah (15:1, 15:8). Oded does not deny that God used Israel to punish Judah; he warns that their cruelty went past what God intended, as Isaiah would say of Assyria (Isaiah 10:5–7). The Law forbade making a fellow Israelite a slave (Leviticus 25:39–46), and the leaders of Ephraim agree with him.

a: They gave them clothes and sandals, food and drink, and rubbed them with oil
p: Men of Samaria clothe and anoint captives, put the weak on donkeys and bring them to Jericho. Jesus' parable echoes it.
b: In Luke 10:30–35 a man going down to Jericho is stripped and left half dead; priest and Levite pass by, and a Samaritan binds his wounds, pours on oil, sets him on his own animal and cares for him. The overlap with this verse is striking: Samaria, Jericho, naked victims, oil, a donkey, care for an enemy. Many commentators, notably F. Scott Spencer, argue Jesus drew on this story. In Chronicles the same point is made: those Judah would call apostate show mercy their southern kin did not expect. Others see only a shared stock of images.

a: the kings of Assyria
p: Kings says Ahaz sent to Tiglath-pileser: 'I am your servant and your son.' Chronicles says only that he asked for help.
b: The Hebrew plural, "kings of Assyria," may be a slip for the singular (the Greek has "the king"), or a general way of speaking. Ahaz's appeal is famous from Isaiah 7, where the prophet urged him to trust God and ask for a sign, and he refused. Tiglath-pileser III's own inscription lists "Jehoahaz of Judah," Ahaz's full name, among the kings who paid him tribute about 734 BC. In Chronicles the word "help" ('azar) runs through the passage: Ahaz seeks help from Assyria and from Damascus's gods, and none comes (28:21, 28:23).

a: Beth-shemesh, Aijalon and Gederoth, Soco with its villages, Timnah with its villages and Gimzo
p: The towns lost lie in the Shephelah, the low hills toward the coast that Uzziah had pushed into.
b: Uzziah's gains against the Philistines (26:6–7) are undone. All the named towns are in the lowland valleys that led from the coast toward Jerusalem: the Sorek valley (Beth-shemesh, Timnah), the Aijalon valley, and the Elah valley (Soco). Gimzo is mentioned only here. The Philistines probably joined the anti-Assyrian alliance and punished Judah for staying out. Tiglath-pileser's campaign of 734 BC went first to Gaza, which fits the timing.

a: He pressed him hard and did not strengthen him
p: Kings says Assyria answered Ahaz and took Damascus. Chronicles says the help was really harm.
b: Both books agree Ahaz paid Assyria with treasure from the temple and palace (2 Kings 16:8). Kings says the plan worked: Tiglath-pilneser took Damascus and killed Rezin (2 Kings 16:9). Chronicles does not deny it, but judges the result. Judah became a vassal with tribute to pay every year, "pressed" (tsar) rather than "made strong" (chazaq). Isaiah had warned that the king of Assyria, called in as a razor for hire, would shave Judah too (Isaiah 7:17–20). The name Tilgath-pilneser is Chronicles' spelling (also 1 Chronicles 5:6, 5:26).
orig: וַיָּצַר לוֹ וְלֹא חֲזָקוֹ (vayyatsar lo velo chazaqo)

a: He sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, who had struck him
p: Kings tells how Ahaz copied an altar from Damascus. Chronicles takes it as worship of Aram's gods.
b: In 2 Kings 16:10–16 Ahaz sees an altar in Damascus, has a copy built and moves the bronze altar aside. Kings does not say outright that it was for foreign gods. Chronicles reads the act as worship of the gods that had beaten him, an irony: he trusts the gods of the winner. Some historians think a vassal had to honor his overlord's gods; Mordechai Cogan argued Assyria did not usually require this, and that Ahaz copied foreign styles by choice. Ahaz's logic, "they will help me," is answered at once: they made him stumble.

a: He closed the doors of the LORD's house
p: Only Chronicles says Ahaz shut the temple. Hezekiah's first act will be to open its doors (29:3).
b: Kings says Ahaz removed the bronze stands and sea and the royal entry "because of the king of Assyria" (2 Kings 16:17–18), but the daily offerings went on at the new altar (2 Kings 16:15). Chronicles goes further: the doors were shut, the lamps out, incense and offerings stopped (29:7). Some historians think Chronicles has made Ahaz's changes total to set up Hezekiah's reopening; others think the main hall may have been closed while worship went on in the court. Either way, the book's story now turns on the doors: shut by Ahaz, opened by his son.

a: They did not bring him into the tombs of Israel's kings
p: Kings says Ahaz was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. Chronicles says not in the royal tombs.
b: Like Jehoram (21:20), Joash (24:25) and Uzziah (26:23), Ahaz is denied the royal tombs. The burial note is one of Chronicles' ways of passing judgment. "Israel's kings" here means Judah's kings, as often in Chronicles, which treats Judah as the true Israel. The Greek reads "in the city of David," closer to Kings.

a: in everything just as his forefather David had done
p: Kings remembers Hezekiah for trust in the Assyrian crisis. Chronicles gives three chapters to his worship reform.
b: 2 Kings 18–20 spends a few lines on Hezekiah's reform and many on Sennacherib. Chronicles reverses the weight: chapters 29–31 tell of the cleansed temple, a Passover for all Israel and the restored priestly gifts; the war takes one chapter (32). Hezekiah is drawn with Solomon's colors: dedication sacrifices, the joy "not since the days of Solomon" (30:26), and an invitation to the northern tribes, as if the divided kingdom could be one again. Hugh Williamson and others see Hezekiah as Chronicles' second Solomon.

a: in the first year of his reign, in the first month
t: The first month of the first year
p: Hezekiah starts at once. The date also lets the cleansing end on Passover eve, which matters in the next chapter.
b: The first month is Nisan, the month of Passover (Exodus 12:2). Kings dates Hezekiah's accession to the third year of Hoshea (2 Kings 18:1), about 727–715 BC depending on the chronology. Chronicles may count his first full year. The temple cleansing takes sixteen days (29:17), passing the 14th, the day for Passover, which explains why the feast had to be held a month late (30:2–3). Whether Chronicles had a dated record or worked the dates from the story is uncertain.

a: From the LORD's tabernacle they turned their faces, and gave it their backs
p: Worship faced the temple. To turn the back on it was a picture of turning from God himself.
b: Hezekiah describes his father's generation in body language. Ezekiel saw men in the temple court "with their backs to the LORD's temple and their faces to the east," bowing to the sun (Ezekiel 8:16). Jeremiah uses the same figure: "They turned their back to me, and not their face" (Jeremiah 2:27; Jeremiah 32:33). The Mishnah records that priests in the Second Temple, at the feast of Booths, turned toward the temple and said, "Our fathers here turned their backs ... but we, our eyes are to the LORD" (Mishnah Sukkah 5:4).

a: something to shudder at, a horror, a thing people hiss at
p: Hezekiah speaks in phrases that Jeremiah later uses of the fall of Jerusalem.
b: "Horror" (shammah) and "hissing" (sheriqah) are a pair found mostly in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 19:8; Jeremiah 25:9; Jeremiah 29:18), and "something to shudder at" (za'avah) too (Jeremiah 15:4; Jeremiah 24:9). People whistled or hissed at a ruin in shock. Hezekiah's sermon thus sounds like the prophets of the exile, a sign that the writer was speaking to readers who knew how the story ended. The written text has lezaw'ah, read as leza'avah; the meaning does not change.
r: Jeremiah 19:8; Jeremiah 24:9; Jeremiah 25:9; Jeremiah 29:18; Deuteronomy 28:25; 1 Kings 9:8

a: Now my heart is set on making a covenant with the LORD
p: Several reforming kings in Chronicles make a covenant: Asa, Jehoiada with Joash, Hezekiah and Josiah.
b: A covenant here is a solemn pledge to keep faith with God, renewing the one made at Sinai. Asa's people "entered into the covenant" (15:12), Jehoiada made one between God, king and people (23:16), and Josiah will read the covenant scroll and make the people stand to it (34:31–32). Hezekiah's covenant is spoken, not described; what follows, cleansing and sacrifice, is its carrying out. The language of "turning back the heat of his anger" returns in 30:8.

a: My sons
p: The king addresses the Levites as a father, or as a teacher addresses pupils.
b: Banai, "my sons," is the language of wisdom teachers (Proverbs 1:8; Proverbs 4:1) and of the prophets' circles. It need not mean Hezekiah was older than the Levites; he was twenty-five. Chronicles' Hezekiah speaks like a teacher of the law as well as a king, and his words draw on Deuteronomy's language for the Levites: chosen "to stand before the LORD to serve him" (Deuteronomy 10:8).

a: Mahath son of Amasai and Joel son of Azariah
p: Fourteen Levites, two each from seven groups: the three Levite clans, Elizaphan, and the three singer families.
b: The list covers Kohath, Merari and Gershon, the classic Levite houses (Numbers 3:17), then Elizaphan, a leading Kohathite family (Numbers 3:30; 1 Chronicles 15:8), then the singers Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun (1 Chronicles 25:1). The names repeat earlier lists in 1 Chronicles 6 and 15, which suggests these were family names handed down. Chronicles treats the singers as full Levites. The readings Jeiel (29:13) and Jehiel (29:14) follow the margin; the written text has Jeuel and Jehuel.

a: the Kidron Wadi
p: Reformers dumped unclean things in the Kidron valley east of the city. Asa and Josiah did the same.
b: The Kidron runs between the temple mount and the Mount of Olives. Asa burned his mother's Asherah image there (15:16), Hezekiah's people throw the incense altars into it (30:14), and Josiah burns the Asherah and scatters its dust on graves there (2 Kings 23:6; 2 Kings 23:12). A valley of tombs and refuse, it was the natural place to remove what defiled the holy place. Note the division of labor: only priests enter the inner house; the Levites carry out what they bring to the court.

a: as a sin offering for the kingdom, for the sanctuary and for Judah
p: The sin offering cleans the altar and the people. Here it covers the kingdom, the temple and Judah.
b: The hatta't, or sin offering, removes impurity from the holy things and guilt from people (Leviticus 4; Leviticus 16). Its rules call for a bull for the community, a goat for a leader (Leviticus 4:13–26). Hezekiah's sevens go beyond any rule, as a sign of completeness. Ezekiel's vision of a new temple also has seven bulls and seven rams daily for the feast (Ezekiel 45:23), and Job offers seven of each (Job 42:8). The ordering, sin offering and then burnt offerings, follows the pattern in Leviticus 9.

a: to make atonement for all Israel
p: The offerings were for all Israel, not just Judah. Northern Israel had fallen or would soon fall to Assyria.
b: "All Israel" is a key phrase for Chronicles. After Samaria fell in 722 BC, many northerners lived under Assyria or fled south; Hezekiah's sacrifice and the Passover invitation (30:1) treat them as part of one people. Critical scholars read this as Chronicles' message for its own day: the people around Jerusalem after the exile should welcome northerners who return to the temple. Christian readers hear in the king's atoning offering for the whole people an image fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 9:11–14).

a: by the command of David, of Gad the king's visionary and of Nathan the prophet
p: Only Chronicles says the temple music was commanded through prophets, as the Law was through Moses.
b: The law of Moses says nothing about singers. Chronicles gives the music its own authority: David arranged it (1 Chronicles 23–26), and God commanded it through Gad and Nathan. The singers themselves "prophesied" with lyres (1 Chronicles 25:1). This made the Levite singers, whose standing rose after the exile, as legitimate as the priests' sacrifices. In the next verses the song begins at the same moment as the burnt offering (29:27), joining sound and sacrifice.

a: with the words of David and of Asaph the visionary
t: The words of David and Asaph
p: The Levites sang psalms. Psalms 50 and 73–83 bear Asaph's name.
b: By the writer's time a body of psalms was linked with David and with Asaph, one of David's three chief singers (1 Chronicles 16:5). Twelve psalms bear Asaph's name (Psalm 50; Psalms 73–83). Calling Asaph a "visionary" (chozeh) fits Chronicles' view of the singers as inspired. 1 Chronicles 16:8–36 shows what such a temple song might be: it quotes parts of Psalms 105, 96 and 106.

a: Now you have given yourselves to the LORD's service
p: The Hebrew is 'you have filled your hand to the LORD', the phrase used for ordaining priests.
b: Mille' yad, "fill the hand," is the technical term for installing a priest (Exodus 28:41; Exodus 29:9), perhaps from placing parts of the offering in his hands (Leviticus 8:27). In 1 Chronicles 29:5 David uses it for the people giving gifts to the temple: "Who will fill his hand today for the LORD?" Here the words are addressed to the assembly, who have consecrated themselves through the offerings, so the Plain gives the sense.

a: The Levites' hearts had been more honest than the priests' about making themselves holy
p: Chronicles praises the Levites over the priests, and lets them do a priest's task in an emergency.
b: The Law gave flaying of burnt offerings to the one who brought it (Leviticus 1:6) or to priests. Here Levites step in. The remark that their hearts were more "upright" (yishrei levav) than the priests' shows the writer's sympathy with the Levites, who in his own time stood below the priests. Some scholars see in this a hint of rivalry in the Second Temple; others a simple account of who was ready. The Greek says the Levites purified themselves "more zealously."

a: for it had all come about in a moment
p: The reform came suddenly. Chronicles credits God, who 'had made it ready' for the people.
b: Sixteen days from shut doors to full worship. Hezekiah and the people rejoice not at their own work but at what God prepared, a note the book often strikes: God makes hearts one (30:12). Jewish readers took the swiftness as a sign of God's favor (Radak). Christian readers have compared such sudden turnings to revival. Critical readers note the compressed time frame as part of the story's idealized picture.

a: He even wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh
p: Hezekiah invites the northern tribes to Jerusalem. Kings says nothing of this Passover.
b: Kings records a great Passover only under Josiah (2 Kings 23:21–23), and says none like it had been kept since the judges. Chronicles alone tells of Hezekiah's, held for "all Israel." Historians are divided. Some accept it: after Samaria fell (722 BC), Hezekiah may have tried to draw the north's survivors to Jerusalem, as Josiah later did by force. Others think Chronicles built the story to give Hezekiah a role like Josiah's and to make a point about reunion. Archaeology shows Jerusalem grew sharply in the late 700s, perhaps with northern refugees.

a: to hold the Passover in the second month
p: The Law allowed a second-month Passover for those unclean or far away. Hezekiah applies it to the whole nation.
b: Numbers 9:9–12 lets anyone unclean from a corpse or away on a journey keep Passover on the 14th of the second month. Here the reasons are the same, extended to everyone: not enough priests were holy, and the people were far off (30:3). The Mishnah, by contrast, remembers Hezekiah as having "intercalated Nisan" (added a second month of Nisan), and lists it among six deeds of his of which the sages did not approve (Mishnah Pesahim 4:9; Bavli Berakhot 10b). Some historians think the date also allowed northerners, who may have used a calendar a month later (1 Kings 12:32), to join.

a: from Beersheba as far as Dan
p: Elsewhere the phrase is 'from Dan to Beersheba'. Chronicles turns it round, starting from Judah.
b: The usual order runs north to south: "from Dan to Beersheba" (Judges 20:1; 1 Samuel 3:20; 2 Samuel 24:2). Chronicles reverses it here and in 1 Chronicles 21:2, as if looking out from Jerusalem. The phrase claims the whole land, including the old north long ruled by Assyria.

a: return to the LORD
p: The letter turns on one Hebrew verb, shuv: return, turn back, bring back. It comes six times in four verses.
b: "Return to the LORD ... so that he may come back" (30:6); "that the heat of his anger turns back" (30:8); "if you return ... and come back to this land ... if you turn back" (30:9). The same verb carries repentance and the return from exile. The prophets use the pairing: "Return to me ... and I will return to you" (Zechariah 1:3; Malachi 3:7). Solomon's prayer had promised that a people who turned back in a land of exile would be heard (6:37–39). The English uses several words where Hebrew has one.

a: will find pity before their captors
p: Hezekiah echoes Solomon's prayer, that captors would treat the exiles with pity.
b: Solomon prayed: "Let their captors look on them with pity and treat them with pity" (1 Kings 8:50); Chronicles has the same in its account of the prayer (6:39). Hezekiah turns the prayer into a promise for northern exiles. The second half of the verse quotes the creed of Exodus 34:6, a God "gracious and compassionate," the order found in later texts (Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Psalm 145:8).
r: 1 Kings 8:50; 2 Chronicles 6:39; Exodus 34:6; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Nehemiah 9:17

a: But people laughed at them and made fun of them
p: Most northerners scorned the call. A few humbled themselves and came.
b: Similar words return at the end of the book, where the people "made fun of God's messengers" (36:16): mal'igim here, the rare mal'ivim there. Chronicles' pattern holds: a call goes out, most refuse, a remnant responds. Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun (30:11), with Ephraim and Issachar (30:18), stand for the north. The scene is often compared with Jesus' parable of the banquet, where those invited make excuses and others come in (Luke 14:16–24).

a: The incense altars too, every one
p: The people remove the altars Ahaz had put on every corner (28:24).
b: The word meqatterot means places for burning, likely incense altars. Small stone horned altars and incense stands are common finds in Iron Age Judah, for instance at Arad, where a shrine with two incense altars was put out of use, perhaps in Hezekiah's or Josiah's reform. The detail joins the people to the king: worship is cleansed by the assembly, not only by royal decree.

a: the priests splashing the blood handed to them by the Levites
p: In the Law each family killed its own Passover lamb. Here Levites slaughter for those who are unclean.
b: Exodus 12:6 has every household slaughter its lamb. Chronicles shows Levites doing it for the unclean (30:17), and under Josiah for everyone (35:6, 35:11). The Passover is becoming a temple sacrifice, with blood splashed on the altar like other offerings. The Mishnah shows the next step: in the Second Temple each owner slaughtered, but priests in rows passed the blood in gold and silver bowls to the altar (Mishnah Pesahim 5:5–6).

a: May the good LORD make atonement for
p: Unclean people ate the Passover, against the Law. Hezekiah prays, and God heals them.
b: Numbers 9:6–13 bars the unclean from eating Passover. Hezekiah asks God to forgive those who set their hearts on seeking him, "even without the cleansing the holy place requires." Jewish tradition treats the episode as an emergency ruling and part of Hezekiah's piety. Christian readers have often pointed to it as a case where the heart counts above ritual purity (compare Mark 7:18–23; 1 Samuel 16:7). Critical scholars see Chronicles balancing respect for the rules with its welcome for northerners. "Healed" (30:20) may mean God held back the illness that uncleanness could bring (Leviticus 15:31).

a: So they kept seven days more
p: Solomon's temple dedication lasted fourteen days. Hezekiah's Passover does too.
b: At the temple's dedication Solomon kept the feast seven days and then seven more (2 Chronicles 7:8–9; 1 Kings 8:65). The gifts of animals also recall Solomon's (7:5). The next verse makes the link plain: nothing like it since Solomon (30:26). Hezekiah reunites what was split after Solomon's death, at least for two weeks.

a: Not since the days of Solomon son of David, king of Israel, had Jerusalem seen anything like it
p: Kings: no Passover like Josiah's since the judges. Chronicles: Hezekiah's was the greatest since Solomon.
b: 2 Kings 23:22 says of Josiah's Passover that none like it had been held since the days of the judges. Chronicles does not contradict this; it gives Josiah a similar line (35:18), but compares Hezekiah's feast only with Solomon's reign. A harmonizing reading says Josiah's was greatest in its keeping of the law, Hezekiah's in its joy and its reunion of north and south. Critical scholars think Chronicles created or enlarged Hezekiah's Passover from Josiah's, giving the earlier king a share of the glory.

a: The Levite priests rose and blessed the people
p: Priests blessed the people with Aaron's words. Some manuscripts and versions read 'the priests and the Levites'.
b: The priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26 was the priests' task (Numbers 6:23; Deuteronomy 10:8). The Hebrew has "the priests the Levites," Deuteronomy's phrase for priests from Levi's tribe; the Greek (Rahlfs) agrees, but many Hebrew manuscripts, the Syriac and the Vulgate read "the priests and the Levites," as in 2 Chronicles 23:18 and 30:15. Chronicles otherwise keeps the two groups distinct, so either reading is possible. Their prayer reached heaven, God's dwelling, as Solomon had asked (6:21).

a: and in Ephraim and Manasseh
p: The worshipers carry the reform into the old northern kingdom, now an Assyrian province.
b: 2 Kings 18:4 says Hezekiah removed the high places and broke the standing stones, without saying where. Chronicles has the people go into Ephraim and Manasseh, Assyrian territory after 722 BC. Some historians doubt Judah could act there; others note Assyrian control of the hill country may have been loose. Josiah's reform later reaches Bethel and Samaria's towns (34:6; 2 Kings 23:15–19).

a: in the gates of the LORD's camps
p: The temple is called 'camps', recalling Israel's camp around the tabernacle in the wilderness.
b: Machanot YHWH, "the camps of the LORD," pictures the temple as the wilderness camp where the Levites guarded the tent (Numbers 2:17; Numbers 3:38). 1 Chronicles 9:18–19 uses the same picture for the gatekeepers. The Dead Sea Scrolls later called Jerusalem "the camp of holiness" (Temple Scroll; 4QMMT).

a: The king's share from his own property was for the burnt offerings
t: The king pays for the daily offerings
p: The king funds the regular burnt offerings. Ezekiel's 'prince' has the same duty.
b: The list follows the calendar of Numbers 28–29: morning and evening, Sabbaths, New Moons and feasts. Ezekiel's vision assigns the same costs to the prince (Ezekiel 45:17), and the Persian kings later paid for offerings in Jerusalem (Ezra 6:9–10; Ezra 7:21–23). Solomon did likewise (8:12–13). The king leads by giving first, and the people follow (31:5).

a: They brought in the tithe of everything, heaps of it
p: The people bring firstfruits and tithes for priests and Levites, as the Law asked.
b: Firstfruits belonged to the priests (Numbers 18:12–13), tithes to the Levites (Numbers 18:21–24), who passed a tenth on to the priests. Honey (31:5) here probably means fruit syrup, especially from dates. The "tithe of cattle and sheep" (31:6) follows Leviticus 27:32. Nehemiah faced the same task after the exile, when the Levites had fled to their fields because the gifts stopped (Nehemiah 13:10–12). Chronicles shows what faithful giving looks like.
r: Numbers 18:12–32; Leviticus 27:30–32; Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Nehemiah 10:35–39; Nehemiah 13:10–12; Malachi 3:10

a: in the third month, and finished in the seventh
p: The heaps grew from the grain harvest in the third month to the fruit harvest in the seventh.
b: The third month holds the Feast of Weeks, the end of the wheat harvest; the seventh holds Booths, the end of the grape and olive harvest (Exodus 23:16; Leviticus 23:15–16, 23:39). The heaps thus took a full harvest season to pile up.

a: Azariah the chief priest, of the house of Zadok
t: Azariah of the house of Zadok
p: A chief priest named Azariah, of Zadok's line. Not the Azariah who stopped Uzziah, perhaps.
b: The chief priest's name matches the priest of 26:17, a generation earlier; Azariah was a common priestly name (1 Chronicles 6:9–13 lists several). Chronicles stresses his descent from Zadok, the line Ezekiel trusted (Ezekiel 44:15). His words, "we have eaten and been full, with plenty left over," echo the blessing promised for faithful giving (Malachi 3:10).

a: from three years old and up
p: Boys were counted from three for food shares. Many emend to 'thirty', the age for service in Numbers.
b: The Hebrew reads three, and the context speaks of men who "came into the LORD's house" for duty, which is odd for toddlers. Numbers 4:3 counts Levites from thirty; 1 Chronicles 23:24 and this chapter (31:17) from twenty. Some scholars think "three" is a slip for "thirty" (shelosh against sheloshim), others that boys from three got rations with their fathers on duty. The Greek and Latin also read three.

a: He did what was good, right and true before the LORD his God
p: The fullest praise in Chronicles. 'Faithful' (emunah) runs through the chapter.
b: The words "good," "right" and "true" (emet) gather Chronicles' praise. The root 'mn, faithfulness, comes three times in this chapter (31:12, 31:15, 31:18) and again in 32:1, "after this faithfulness." The king's faithfulness is set right before the invasion, so the reader knows the threat is not a punishment.

a: After these things and this faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came
t: Why does trouble come to a faithful king?
p: Chronicles usually ties trouble to sin. Here it says outright that the invasion came after faithfulness.
b: Chronicles is known for linking blessing to obedience and disaster to sin, often within one reign. Sennacherib's attack breaks the pattern, and the writer takes care to say so. The invasion becomes a test, like the trials of Asa (14:9) and Jehoshaphat (20:1), which faith overcomes. Kings tells the story differently: it places the invasion in Hezekiah's fourteenth year, includes his tribute and stripping of the temple doors (2 Kings 18:13–16), and Chronicles leaves both out. Sennacherib's annals confirm the tribute.

a: they stopped up all the springs and the stream that ran through the middle of the land
p: Besiegers needed water. Hezekiah's people blocked springs outside the walls and kept water inside.
b: Isaiah mentions collecting the waters of the lower pool and making a reservoir between the walls (Isaiah 22:9–11), and rebukes the planners for not looking to God who made it. The plural "kings of Assyria" in the people's words may be a general way of speaking. The "stream" may be the overflow from Gihon running down the Kidron valley.

a: with another wall outside it
p: A wall seven meters thick, found in Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter, is widely linked with Hezekiah.
b: In 1970 Nahman Avigad uncovered a stretch of wall about 7 meters (23 feet) thick, built across houses of the late 700s BC, west of the old City of David. It is usually dated to Hezekiah and connected with the "Broad Wall" of Nehemiah 3:8 and with Isaiah's taunt that houses were torn down to strengthen the wall (Isaiah 22:10). The city had spread west onto the western hill, perhaps with refugees from the north. The Millo was an earthwork or terrace in the City of David (1 Kings 9:15).

a: He has an arm of flesh
p: Hezekiah contrasts human strength with God's. Jeremiah uses the same phrase.
b: Jeremiah curses the one "who makes flesh his arm" and turns from the LORD (Jeremiah 17:5). Isaiah says Egypt's horses are flesh, not spirit (Isaiah 31:3). The picture recalls Elisha's words to his servant: "There are more with us than with them" (2 Kings 6:16), which Hezekiah echoes in 32:7. Christian hymns and sermons have long used "the arm of flesh" for misplaced trust.

a: while Sennacherib king of Assyria was at Lachish
p: Lachish, Judah's second city, fell to Sennacherib. His palace reliefs show the siege.
b: Chronicles cuts the long speech of 2 Kings 18:17–35 to a few verses but keeps Lachish. Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh had a room of reliefs showing the siege and capture of Lachish, now in the British Museum. Excavations found the Assyrian siege ramp, the Judean counter-ramp, arrowheads and a mass burial. It is one of the best-documented sieges of the ancient world.

a: You must bow down in front of one altar
p: The Assyrians use Hezekiah's reform against him: he closed the LORD's own shrines.
b: The Rabshakeh's argument (also in 2 Kings 18:22) takes for granted that many altars honored a god more. Hezekiah's centralizing reform could look to locals like an insult to the LORD. Critical scholars use this verse as evidence that a reform under Hezekiah was remembered, though some think it was read back from Josiah's time. Excavations at Arad and Beersheba show shrines dismantled in the late 700s BC, which many date to Hezekiah.

a: things that human hands had made
p: Chronicles' own comment: the Assyrians spoke of Israel's God as if he were an idol.
b: In Kings, Hezekiah's prayer makes this point: the gods of the nations were "only things that human hands had made out of wood and stone" (2 Kings 19:18). Chronicles leaves out the prayer's words and puts the judgment in the narrator's mouth. The prophets often mock idols in these terms (Isaiah 44:9–20; Psalm 115:4).

a: Hezekiah the king and Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet, prayed about this
p: In Kings, Hezekiah prays and Isaiah answers with an oracle. Here both pray together.
b: Kings has Hezekiah send to Isaiah, then spread Sennacherib's letter in the temple and pray, and Isaiah send a long oracle (2 Kings 19:1–34). Chronicles reduces this to one line in which king and prophet pray side by side. The picture fits Chronicles' ideal of king and prophet working as one. The Greek text and some readers take the two as joint intercessors; Jewish tradition remembers Isaiah's prayer as well.

a: Then the LORD sent an angel
p: Kings says the angel struck 185,000 in one night. Chronicles gives no number. Assyria's own records claim victory.
b: 2 Kings 19:35 numbers the dead at 185,000. Chronicles speaks of every warrior, leader and commander, without a number. Sennacherib's annals say he shut Hezekiah up "like a bird in a cage" and received tribute, but do not claim to have taken Jerusalem. Herodotus heard from Egyptian priests that mice ate the Assyrians' bowstrings near Egypt (Histories 2.141), which some link to plague. Most historians agree the siege was lifted and Jerusalem survived. Sennacherib was murdered by his sons in 681 BC, twenty years later, as Babylonian chronicles confirm; Chronicles joins the events for its point.

a: and gave him a sign
p: Chronicles only alludes to the story told in 2 Kings 20 and Isaiah 38: the shadow going back ten steps.
b: Chronicles regularly assumes readers know Kings. In 2 Kings 20:1–11 Isaiah tells the sick Hezekiah he will die; the king weeps and prays, and God adds fifteen years, with the sign of the shadow moving back on the stairway of Ahaz. Chronicles mentions the sign again in 32:31, where the Babylonian envoys come to ask about it, a detail Kings does not give. The Babylonians, famous astronomers, would have been interested in such a sign.

a: But Hezekiah did not pay back the good done to him
p: Kings tells of Hezekiah showing his treasures to Babylon. Chronicles calls it pride and says he humbled himself.
b: In 2 Kings 20:12–19 Hezekiah shows his storehouses to the Babylonian envoys, Isaiah foretells the exile, and Hezekiah answers, "Will there not be peace in my days?" Chronicles names the fault, "his heart rose up high," the phrase used of Uzziah (26:16), and then adds that he humbled himself, so that wrath was delayed until after him (32:26). This reads Kings' ambiguous reply as repentance. Jewish tradition faulted Hezekiah for not singing a song of praise after his rescue (Bavli Sanhedrin 94a).

a: stopped up the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and led them straight down, westward
p: A 533-meter tunnel carries Gihon's water under the City of David to Siloam. An inscription tells how it was dug.
b: Kings mentions "the pool and the channel" (2 Kings 20:20). The tunnel was found in the 1800s; in 1880 an inscription was discovered inside describing the moment the two teams of diggers met. Radiocarbon dating of plant matter in the plaster supports a date around 700 BC (Frumkin and others, 2003), though some argue for an earlier start. The inscription is now in Istanbul. Sirach praises Hezekiah for bringing water into the city (Sirach 48:17).

a: God left him, to test him and to know all that was in his heart
p: God 'left' Hezekiah to test him, the language Deuteronomy uses of the wilderness years.
b: Moses told Israel that God led them in the wilderness "to humble you and to test you, to know what was in your heart" (Deuteronomy 8:2). Chronicles applies this to one king. God does not abandon him for good; he withdraws for a moment so that what is in the heart is shown. Readers have compared it with God's testing of Abraham (Genesis 22:1) and with the Lord's Prayer: "And do not bring us into testing" (Matthew 6:13).

a: in the vision of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz
p: The book of Isaiah calls itself 'the vision of Isaiah son of Amoz' (Isaiah 1:1).
b: Isaiah 36–39 contains almost the same account of Hezekiah as 2 Kings 18–20. Chronicles may cite the prophetic book, or a section of the royal annals that included it. The Greek reads "in the prophecy of Isaiah ... and in the book of the kings," as two works. Either way, the book points readers to a prophet as the source.

a: on the rise where the tombs of David's descendants are
p: Hezekiah is buried in the 'ascent' of the royal tombs, perhaps the highest place of honor.
b: Ma'aleh can mean "ascent" or "upper part." Rabbinic tradition took it as the most honored spot, beside David and Solomon, and said a Torah scroll was laid on his bier (Bavli Bava Qamma 16b). From Hezekiah on, Kings stops recording royal burials "with his ancestors in the City of David"; Manasseh and Amon are buried in a garden (2 Kings 21:18, 21:26).

a: he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem
p: Manasseh ruled longer than any other king of Judah or Israel, about 697–642 BC.
b: The fifty-five years probably include a co-regency with Hezekiah. Assyrian records name "Manasseh king of Judah" twice: among twenty-two western kings who sent building materials to Esarhaddon for his palace at Nineveh (about 676 BC), and among kings who marched with Ashurbanipal's army against Egypt (about 667 BC). He was a loyal vassal through Assyria's peak. Kings judges him the worst king of all; Chronicles agrees about his early reign but tells a different ending (33:12–16).

a: He put up altars for the Baals and made Asherah poles
p: Kings has 'altars for Baal' and 'an Asherah pole, just like Ahab'. Chronicles makes both plural and drops Ahab.
b: 2 Kings 21:3 compares Manasseh with Ahab, the northern king who served Baal. Chronicles has plurals, "the Baals" and "Asherah poles," as it did for Ahaz (28:2), and leaves out the comparison. The plural is a general term for false gods, used often in Judges and Chronicles. Dropping Ahab may keep the focus on Judah, whose kings Chronicles judges by their own standard.

a: He made his sons pass through the fire
p: Kings has 'his son'. Chronicles has 'his sons', as with Ahaz (28:3).
b: 2 Kings 21:6 says Manasseh made "his son" pass through the fire. Chronicles has the plural, and adds "in the Valley of Ben-hinnom," the place Jeremiah later named as the site of child sacrifice at Topheth (Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 19:5–6). The list of occult practices follows Deuteronomy 18:10–11, where each is forbidden. The Plain renders ov and yidde'oni as "ghosts of the dead" and "spirits that know things," the site's terms.

a: the carved image of the figure
p: Kings says Manasseh set 'the carved image of the Asherah' in the temple. Chronicles calls it 'the figure'.
b: Chronicles uses semel, a rare word for an image or statue, in place of Kings' "Asherah" (2 Kings 21:7). Ezekiel speaks of "the figure of jealousy" at the temple's north gate (Ezekiel 8:3–5), and Deuteronomy forbids an idol "in the form of any figure" (Deuteronomy 4:16). Chronicles may avoid naming the goddess or may be using Ezekiel's word. In 33:15 Manasseh himself removes the figure, a reversal Kings does not record.

a: Never again will I remove Israel's feet from the soil I appointed for your ancestors
p: Kings has God promise never again to send Israel's feet wandering from the soil he gave their ancestors.
b: 2 Kings 21:8 uses lehaniyd, "to make wander," and "I gave"; Chronicles has lehasir, "to remove," and "I appointed," with "your ancestors." The ending differs too: Kings has "the law that my servant Moses laid on them," Chronicles "the whole law, the rules and the rulings given through Moses." The sense is close; Chronicles' wording is its own, so the Plain differs from Kings here.

a: The LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they would not listen
p: Kings quotes the prophets' warning in full. Chronicles sums it up in one line and adds what came next.
b: 2 Kings 21:10–15 gives the oracle: God will wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish and turns it upside down. Chronicles leaves out the doom, which for Kings explains the exile, and goes straight to Manasseh's capture, which Kings never mentions. A Jewish tradition held that Manasseh killed Isaiah, who was sawn in two inside a cedar (Bavli Yevamot 49b; the Martyrdom of Isaiah), a story often seen behind Hebrews 11:37.

a: They caught Manasseh with hooks, bound him in bronze fetters and led him off to Babylon
p: Only Chronicles tells of Manasseh's arrest. No Assyrian record mentions it, but there are real parallels.
b: Several points make the story possible. Assyrian kings did lead captives by hooks in the nose or lip (compare 2 Kings 19:28; Ezekiel 19:4), and Esarhaddon's stele at Zincirli shows two captives so held. Ashurbanipal's brother Shamash-shum-ukin, king of Babylon, revolted in 652–648 BC with western allies; a vassal suspected of joining could have been summoned to Babylon after its fall. Necho I of Sais, father of Psamtik I, was taken in chains to Nineveh, then pardoned and sent home (Ashurbanipal's Rassam Cylinder). Other historians judge the story a theological creation to explain Manasseh's long reign. The question is open.

a: Before the God of his ancestors he humbled himself deeply
p: Kings blames Manasseh for the exile itself. Chronicles says he humbled himself and was restored.
b: 2 Kings 21:11–16, 23:26 and 24:3–4 say that because of Manasseh's sins the LORD would not turn from his anger, even after Josiah. Chronicles never says this. Instead Manasseh is its clearest proof that repentance works: the worst king prays and is heard. Jewish tradition argued: the Mishnah lists Manasseh among kings with no share in the world to come, but Rabbi Judah disagreed, citing this verse (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2), and the Talmud has God accept him despite the angels' objection. Christian readers have taken him as a model penitent. Critical scholars see Chronicles adjusting history to its rule that each generation answers for itself.

a: and God was entreated by him
p: The verb means 'let himself be entreated'. A rabbinic pun read it as 'dug through'.
b: Vayye'ater lo, "he was entreated by him," comes from 'atar, to plead or be pleaded with. The Jerusalem Talmud reads it as if written vayyechater, "he dug," and tells how the angels shut the windows of heaven against Manasseh's prayer, so God dug an opening under his throne to receive it (Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 10:2). The Targum of Chronicles tells that Manasseh was put in a bronze mule over a fire, cried in vain to his idols, then called on the LORD and was heard. The legends show how hard it was to accept that God forgave Manasseh, and how firmly the tradition held that he did.

a: Then Manasseh came to know that the LORD, he is God
p: Manasseh confesses in the words the people cried at Mount Carmel.
b: When fire fell on Elijah's altar the people cried, "The LORD, he is the God!" (1 Kings 18:39). Manasseh, who built Baal's altars like Ahab (2 Kings 21:3), comes to the same confession. The phrase also recalls Deuteronomy 4:35, 39.

a: he built an outside wall to the City of David
p: After his return Manasseh builds walls and garrisons, the marks of a blessed king in Chronicles.
b: Building and fortifying are signs of God's favor in Chronicles (11:5–12; 26:9–10; 27:3–4). Manasseh's wall, on the west of Gihon in the Kidron valley, has been linked by some archaeologists with walls found on the eastern slope of the City of David from the 600s BC. The Fish Gate stood on the north side (Nehemiah 3:3). A strong Judah in the mid-600s also fits Assyrian policy, which wanted a loyal buffer toward Egypt.

a: though only to the LORD their God
p: Even after Manasseh's reform, the people worshiped at local shrines, though now to the LORD.
b: Chronicles' reform is real but partial: the shrines stay, as under Asa and Jehoshaphat (15:17; 20:33). This explains why Josiah still has work to do. The view that local sacrifice to the LORD was wrong but less grave than idolatry matches Kings' judgment on earlier kings (1 Kings 3:2–3).

a: his prayer to his God
p: A short penitential prayer in Manasseh's name survives in Greek. Orthodox Christians count it as Scripture.
b: The Prayer of Manasseh, fifteen verses long, was probably composed in Greek or Hebrew between the 200s BC and AD 100. It is found among the Odes appended to the Psalms in Codex Alexandrinus and quoted in the third-century Didascalia Apostolorum. The Orthodox churches include it in their Bible; the Latin Vulgate printed it in an appendix; Protestant Bibles that include the Apocrypha place it there; the Jewish canon lacks it. A Hebrew poem from Qumran (4Q381 33:8–11) is titled "Prayer of Manasseh king of Judah when the king of Assyria imprisoned him," a separate composition. Both show readers wanting the words Chronicles mentions.

a: the records of Hozai
p: The Hebrew has an unknown name, Hozai. The Greek reads 'the seers', as in the verse before.
b: Chozai could be a proper name, otherwise unknown, or a slip for hachozim, "the visionaries," mentioned in 33:18. The Greek and many modern versions read "the seers." One Hebrew manuscript has chozav, "his visionaries." The Plain keeps the Hebrew; see the variant.

a: they buried him at his house
p: Kings says Manasseh was buried 'in the garden of his house, in the garden of Uzza'.
b: 2 Kings 21:18 names the garden of Uzza, and Amon is buried there too (2 Kings 21:26). Chronicles shortens the note. The Greek of Chronicles reads "in the garden of his house," closer to Kings. Burial outside the tombs of the kings, in Chronicles' usual pattern, would mark disapproval; here it simply follows Kings.

a: Before the LORD he did not humble himself
p: Chronicles measures Amon by his father's humbling, not his father's sins.
b: Kings says Amon "walked the whole road his father had walked" (2 Kings 21:21). Chronicles adds a contrast: Manasseh humbled himself, Amon did not. "Humble oneself" (nikhna') is a key word in Chronicles (7:14; 12:6–7; 32:26; 34:27). The name Amon may echo the Egyptian god Amun, perhaps a sign of Egyptian ties, though it can also be Hebrew for "faithful" or "craftsman."

a: Then the people of the land killed everyone
p: A group of Judah's landholders who backed the house of David, putting Joash, Josiah and Jehoahaz on the throne.
b: 'Am ha'arets in Kings and Chronicles is a political group of free landowners in Judah, as against the court in Jerusalem. They acted at Joash's crowning (23:20–21), here after Amon's murder, and again for Jehoahaz (36:1). After the exile the same phrase came to mean outsiders or the unlearned (Ezra 4:4), a sense very different from this one.

a: When he had reigned eight years, and was still a young man, he began to seek the God of his forefather David
p: Kings puts the whole reform after the scroll is found in Josiah's 18th year. Chronicles starts it in his 8th and 12th.
b: In 2 Kings 22–23 the scroll's discovery sets off the reform. Chronicles has Josiah seek God at sixteen, begin purging at twenty, and only then find the scroll (34:8, 34:14). This fits Chronicles' view that the king's heart came first, and it may preserve a memory that the reform grew over time. Historians note that Assyria's grip weakened after Ashurbanipal's death (about 631 BC), around Josiah's twelfth year, which would have left him free to act. Others think Chronicles simply rearranged Kings so that the cleansing comes before the Passover.

a: Priests' bones he burned on their altars
p: A man of God had foretold under Jeroboam that a king named Josiah would burn priests' bones on Bethel's altar.
b: In 1 Kings 13:2 a prophet from Judah cries against Jeroboam's altar: "On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places, who burn their incense on you. They will burn people's bones on you." Kings tells the fulfillment at Bethel (2 Kings 23:15–20). Chronicles moves the bone-burning into its summary and does not mention Bethel, though its readers knew the story.

a: and in the ruined places around them
p: The Hebrew is hard. Read one way it says 'with their swords'; read another, 'in their ruins'.
b: The written text (Ketiv) has two words, behar battehem, perhaps "in the hill country of their houses." The margin (Qere) reads one word, bchrbtyhm, which the Masoretes pointed becharvoteihem, "with their swords." With other vowels the same letters give bechorvoteihem, "in their ruins," which suits the northern towns wasted by Assyria (compare Ezekiel 33:24). The Greek has "in their places round about." The Plain follows the consonants of the margin with the vowels for "ruins"; see the variant.

a: had gathered it from the hands of Manasseh and Ephraim and all the rest of Israel
p: Chronicles adds that money came from northern Israel too, again making Josiah's temple belong to all Israel.
b: 2 Kings 22:4 says the doorkeepers collected silver "from the people." Chronicles names the givers: Manasseh, Ephraim, "all the rest of Israel" and Judah and Benjamin. Archaeology has found a few Judean items in the old north from this time, which some read as signs of Josiah's reach; others think his rule there was limited to Bethel. The written text has "the people of Jerusalem" (veyoshvei); the margin reads "and they returned to Jerusalem" (vayyashuvu). The Plain follows the written text here, with the Greek; see the variant.

a: every one who knew how to play instruments of song
p: Only Chronicles has the Levite musicians among the overseers of the builders.
b: The Hebrew is brief: the musicians were among the Levites over the work. Some take it to mean only that skilled Levites oversaw the workers; others imagine music to set the pace, as with ancient work songs, though the text does not say so. It is another sign of Chronicles' interest in the Levites, who here even serve as scribes and officials (34:13).

a: Hilkiah the priest came upon the scroll of the LORD's law, given by the hand of Moses
p: Chronicles calls it 'the scroll of the LORD's law, by the hand of Moses'. What was it?
b: Most scholars since W. M. L. de Wette (1805) identify the scroll with a core of Deuteronomy: its curses (34:24), its demand for one place of worship, and the reform's details match. Many critical scholars think it was written shortly before, in the circles of reformers, and "found" to give it authority; others think it was an older book lost under Manasseh. Chronicles makes the claim explicit with "by the hand of Moses." Medieval Jewish commentators held that it was the temple's own Torah scroll, hidden during the evil reigns, and that it was found open at the curse of exile for king and people (Deuteronomy 28:36). See 2 Kings 22:8.

a: Huldah, a woman prophet
p: Huldah is one of a few women called prophets in the Hebrew Bible. Kings and Chronicles tell her story alike.
b: She is consulted even though Jeremiah and Zephaniah were active (Jeremiah 1:2; Zephaniah 1:1). The Talmud asks why and suggests women are more compassionate (Bavli Megillah 14b), and counts her among seven women prophets. The southern gates of the temple mount were later known as the Huldah Gates (Mishnah Middot 1:3), which some link with her. Her husband's ancestry differs from Kings, where he is son of Tikvah, son of Harhas; the differences are copying variants (see the variant).

a: all the curses written in the scroll
p: Kings has 'all the words of the scroll'. Chronicles says 'all the curses', pointing to Deuteronomy 28.
b: Deuteronomy ends its covenant with blessings and long curses for disobedience, ending in exile (Deuteronomy 28:15–68; Deuteronomy 29:20–27). Chronicles makes the link explicit, as Josiah's scroll seems to be the one that "curses" a people who forsake God. Leviticus 26 has a similar list.

a: You humbled yourself before God
t: Humbled, before God and before me
p: Chronicles says 'you humbled yourself' twice, 'before God' and 'before me'. Kings says it once, 'before the LORD'.
b: Both books use the verb nikhna', "humble oneself," a key word in Chronicles (7:14; 12:6; 32:26; 33:12; 33:23), and the site renders it the same way in both. Kings has "before the LORD" and goes on to quote God's threat that the land would become "a ruin and a curse" (2 Kings 22:19). Chronicles has "before God," drops the threat, and repeats the verb: "you humbled yourself before me." The repetition links Josiah with Manasseh, who humbled himself, and sets him against Amon and Zedekiah, who did not (33:23; 36:12).

a: You will be gathered into your grave in peace
p: Josiah was killed in battle. Was Huldah's promise of a peaceful death kept?
b: Josiah died of wounds at Megiddo (35:23–24). Interpreters answer in several ways. Many read "in peace" as he would not see the city's fall, which is explained in the next line. Some Jewish commentators hold that he died in peace with God, having been mourned; others that he forfeited the promise by ignoring Neco's warning, as Chronicles implies (35:22). Critical scholars suggest the prophecy was spoken before his death and left unchanged because it was remembered as true, a sign it was not invented later.

a: the priests and the Levites
p: Kings lists 'the priests and the prophets' at the reading. Chronicles has 'the priests and the Levites'.
b: 2 Kings 23:2 places prophets in the crowd. Chronicles, which often calls Levites prophets (1 Chronicles 25:1), names the Levites instead. It may reflect a different Kings text, or the writer's view of who carried the word in the temple. The Greek also has Levites.

a: The king stood in his place
p: Kings says 'by the pillar'. Chronicles says 'in his place'.
b: Kings has Josiah stand "by the pillar" (2 Kings 23:3; compare 2 Kings 11:14), and Chronicles has "his place" ('omdo), perhaps the royal platform of 6:13. The covenant language is Deuteronomy's: all the heart and all the being (Deuteronomy 6:5).

a: Josiah held a Passover for the LORD in Jerusalem
p: Kings gives Josiah's Passover three verses. Chronicles gives it nineteen, and 1 Esdras begins its book with it.
b: 2 Kings 23:21–23 says only that the king commanded it "by what is written in this covenant scroll" and that none like it had been kept since the judges. Chronicles describes the roles of king, priests, Levites and singers in detail, and on the proper date, the fourteenth of the first month, unlike Hezekiah's. The Greek book called 1 Esdras (in the Septuagint as Esdras A) opens with this Passover (1 Esdras 1:1–20) and goes on through the end of Chronicles into Ezra, so it is an early witness to these chapters. References to 1 Esdras in these notes follow the numbering of Swete's Greek text; the KJV Apocrypha numbers most of chapter 1 two or three verses higher.

a: Set the ark of holiness in the house that Solomon son of David, king of Israel, built
p: Why must the ark be put back in the temple? The verse is a puzzle, and it gave rise to legends.
b: Several answers have been given. Some scholars think Manasseh or Amon had removed the ark and Josiah restored it. Others read the command loosely: since the ark now rests in the temple and need not be carried (1 Chronicles 23:26), the Levites should turn to other service. Jewish tradition took it the opposite way: Josiah ordered the ark hidden, foreseeing the exile, in a chamber Solomon had built (Bavli Yoma 52b; Bavli Horayot 12a; Tosefta Sotah 13:1), and it never returned to the Second Temple. Another tradition says Jeremiah hid it in a cave on Mount Nebo (2 Maccabees 2:4–8). For "who taught," the written text has hammevunim and the margin hammevinim, with little change of sense.

a: They came to thirty thousand, with three thousand cattle
p: Josiah gives 30,000 small animals and 3,000 cattle, about ten times Hezekiah's gift (30:24).
b: The number of lambs and kids roughly fits a large gathering. Josephus says a Passover animal was shared by a group of at least ten, and reports a count of 255,600 victims in his own day (Jewish War 6.423–425). The cattle were for the festival's other sacrifices (Deuteronomy 16:2 allows "the flock and the herd"). Like Hezekiah (31:3), the king pays first and his officials follow.

a: They cooked the Passover in the fire, by the rule
p: Exodus says roast the lamb, not boil it. Deuteronomy says 'cook' it. Chronicles combines the two.
b: Exodus 12:9 commands: "Do not eat any of it raw, or boiled at all in water, but roasted over fire." Deuteronomy 16:7 says simply "Cook it," using bashal, the verb usually used for boiling. Chronicles writes vayevashshelu ... ba'esh, "they cooked ... in the fire," joining Deuteronomy's verb to Exodus' fire, while the other holy offerings are "cooked in pots." Michael Fishbane and others take this as an early example of reconciling two laws in one practice, a method later developed by the rabbis. Rabbinic law follows Exodus: the Passover lamb must be roasted (Mishnah Pesahim 7:1).

a: Jeduthun the king's visionary
p: The singers and gatekeepers did not leave their posts, since the Levites prepared their portions for them.
