b: The scene shows a whole temple staff in order, each group at its task. Calling Jeduthun a "visionary," like Gad and Asaph (29:25, 29:30), fits Chronicles' view that temple music was prophetic (1 Chronicles 25:1–5). In 1 Chronicles 25:5 Heman too is "the king's visionary."

a: since the days of Samuel the prophet
p: Kings says 'since the days of the judges'. Chronicles says 'since Samuel'.
b: The two phrases point to the same era, as Samuel was the last of the judges (1 Samuel 7:15). Chronicles likes Samuel as a founder of temple service (1 Chronicles 9:22; 1 Chronicles 26:28). After praising Hezekiah's Passover as the greatest since Solomon (30:26), Chronicles keeps Kings' claim for Josiah: his was the finest in its keeping of the law.

a: It was in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign that this Passover was held
p: After this verse the Greek inserts four verses on Josiah's reform and the LORD's anger, taken from 2 Kings 23:24–27.
b: The Septuagint of Chronicles has verses 19a–d: Josiah removed the mediums, the teraphim and the idols to fulfill the law; there was no king like him; yet the LORD did not turn from his anger because of Manasseh. These match 2 Kings 23:24–27. 1 Esdras 1:21–22 has a shorter note on Josiah's upright heart and the sins of the earlier generation. Most scholars think the Greek supplied the lines from Kings; Chronicles itself avoids blaming Manasseh (see 33:12). See the variant.

a: up came Neco king of Egypt to make war at Carchemish on the Euphrates
p: In 609 BC Pharaoh Neco II marched north to help the last Assyrian forces. Josiah tried to stop him.
b: Kings says Neco marched up "toward the king of Assyria, to the Euphrates River" (2 Kings 23:29). The Babylonian Chronicle shows that in 609 BC Egypt came to aid Ashur-uballit II, Assyria's last king, in his attempt to retake Harran. Chronicles names Carchemish, where the decisive battle was fought four years later (Jeremiah 46:2), perhaps by an adjustment to the better-known site. 1 Esdras 1:23 reads "Carchamis upon Euphrates"; the Greek of Chronicles says Neco went "against the king of the Assyrians." Josiah's motive is unknown; he may have sided with Babylon.

a: God bade me hurry
p: Chronicles says God really did speak through the pharaoh, and Josiah's death followed from not listening.
b: Neco claims a divine order, and the narrator agrees (35:22: "Neco's words from God's mouth"). Kings offers no reason for Josiah's death, a hard fact for its theology. Chronicles supplies one: even a good king fell when he did not listen. 1 Esdras softens it: Josiah ignored "the words of Jeremiah the prophet from the mouth of the Lord" (1 Esdras 1:26). The Talmud says Josiah misread Leviticus 26:6, thinking no sword would pass through a faithful land (Bavli Taanit 22b). Christian readers have noted that God's word can come through unexpected people (compare Numbers 22:28; John 11:51).

a: He disguised himself to fight him
p: Josiah's death is told with phrases from Ahab's: a disguise, an archer, 'get me out, I am wounded'.
b: Ahab said, "I will disguise myself and go into the battle" (1 Kings 22:30); an arrow struck him, and he told his driver to take him out of the fight, for he was wounded (1 Kings 22:34; 2 Chronicles 18:33). Josiah also "disguised himself" and says, "Get me away from here. I am hurt very badly" (35:23). The echoes cast Josiah, at his end, as a king who would not hear a prophet's word. The Greek has "strengthened himself" (perhaps reading hitchazzeq for hitchappes), and 1 Esdras "undertook to fight"; see the variant.

a: in the valley of Megiddo
p: Megiddo guarded the main pass through the Carmel range. The name lies behind 'Armageddon' (Revelation 16:16).
b: Megiddo was a fortress on the international road between Egypt and Mesopotamia, scene of many battles from Thutmose III (about 1457 BC) on. Josiah's death there became a byword for national mourning: Zechariah compares a future grief to "the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo" (Zechariah 12:11). Revelation's "Armageddon," "the mountain of Megiddo," draws on this memory of a decisive battlefield.

a: drove him to Jerusalem. There he died
p: Kings says Neco killed Josiah at Megiddo and his body was brought home. Chronicles says he died in Jerusalem.
b: 2 Kings 23:29–30 says Neco "put him to death" at Megiddo when he saw him, and his servants carried his dead body to Jerusalem. Chronicles has him wounded in battle and taken in a second chariot to Jerusalem, where he died. 1 Esdras 1:29 agrees with Chronicles. The two can be read together (mortally wounded at Megiddo, died on the way or on arrival), or as different traditions. Chronicles' version keeps his death in the city, in some sense "in peace" with his ancestors, as Huldah said (34:28).

a: Jeremiah sang a lament over Josiah
p: Jeremiah lamented Josiah, and the laments were written in 'the Laments'. Is this the book of Lamentations?
b: No lament for Josiah survives by name. Jewish tradition identified "the Laments" (haqqinot) with the book of Lamentations, and some read Lamentations 4:20, "the breath of our nostrils, the LORD's anointed, was trapped in their pits," as about Josiah (Targum to Lamentations 4:20; Josephus, Antiquities 10.78). Most modern scholars think Lamentations mourns Jerusalem's fall in 587 BC, and that the collection named here is lost. Jeremiah did speak of Josiah warmly (Jeremiah 22:10, 22:15–16). On the yearly mourning, see Zechariah 12:11.

a: Jehoahaz
p: Josiah's son is Jehoahaz in 36:1 and the shorter Joahaz in 36:2 and 36:4. Jeremiah calls him Shallum.
b: The Hebrew spells the name in full in 36:1 and in short form in the next verses; the site keeps each verse's spelling. Jeremiah 22:11 calls him Shallum, probably his birth name, Jehoahaz being a throne name; 1 Chronicles 3:15 lists a Shallum as Josiah's fourth son. Chronicles drops Kings' notes on the mothers of the last four kings and on their being evil "just as his ancestors had done", except for the evil itself in 36:5, 36:9 and 36:12.

a: he reigned three months in Jerusalem
p: The Greek inserts Jehoahaz's mother, his evil, and his imprisonment at Riblah, all from 2 Kings 23:31–33.
b: The Septuagint has extra verses here (36:2a–c), and again after 36:4 and 36:5, that supply what Kings has and Chronicles lacks: Jehoahaz's mother Amital (Hamutal) of Libnah, Neco binding him at Riblah ("Deblatha"), Jehoahaz's death in Egypt and Jehoiakim's taxing of the land (36:4a), Jehoiakim's mother Zechora (36:5), and his three years of service to Nebuchadnezzar with raids by Chaldeans and others. Most scholars think the translators or later editors filled the gaps from Kings. 1 Esdras 1:32–38 follows the shorter Hebrew. See the variants at 36:2, 36:4 and 36:5.

a: bound him in bronze fetters to take him to Babylon
p: Kings says Jehoiakim died and his son succeeded. Chronicles says he was chained to be taken to Babylon.
b: 2 Kings 24:6 says only that he "lay down with his ancestors." Jeremiah foretold he would have "the burial of a donkey" outside the gates (Jeremiah 22:18–19; Jeremiah 36:30). Daniel 1:1–2 says Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem in Jehoiakim's third year and the Lord gave Jehoiakim into his hand, with some temple vessels. The Greek of Chronicles and 1 Esdras 1:38 say he was taken to Babylon. The Hebrew can mean Nebuchadnezzar intended to take him, but did not. Historians note the Babylonian Chronicle records Nebuchadnezzar in the west in 604–601 BC and his capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC, after Jehoiakim's death. Harmonizers suggest he was bound, then released as a vassal.

a: he put them in his temple in Babylon
p: The temple's articles go to Babylon in three stages. Their return matters to Ezra and Daniel.
b: Chronicles traces the vessels: some under Jehoiakim (36:7), the precious ones under Jehoiachin (36:10), the rest in 586 BC (36:18). Heikhal can mean a palace or a temple; Daniel 1:2 says they were put "in the treasury of that god's house," and Belshazzar later drinks from them (Daniel 5:2–4). Ezra 1:7–11 lists them coming back under Cyrus. For Chronicles, the vessels link the first temple with the second: worship would continue with the very things David and Solomon provided.

a: what was found against him
p: A rabbinic tradition took 'what was found on him' literally: tattoos with the names of idols.
b: The Hebrew vehannimtsa' 'alav, "what was found against him" or "on him," most likely refers to his crimes. Rabbis debated it: one said he had the name of an idol tattooed on his body (Bavli Sanhedrin 103b; Leviticus Rabbah 19:6). The Greek has "all that he did" and then a burial notice: Jehoiakim lay down with his ancestors "and was buried in Ganoza" (ἐν Γανοζα), probably a transliteration of "the garden of Uzza" (2 Kings 21:18; 2 Kings 21:26). The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: Jehoiachin was eight years old when he became king
p: Kings says Jehoiachin was eighteen. The Hebrew of Chronicles says eight. Most think 'ten' dropped out.
b: 2 Kings 24:8 has eighteen, and the next verses mention his wives (2 Kings 24:15), which suits eighteen. The Greek in Rahlfs' edition (with Alexandrinus and the Lucianic manuscripts), the Syriac and some Hebrew manuscripts read eighteen; only Codex Vaticanus has eight, like the Hebrew. 1 Esdras 1:41 is split the same way: Codex Vaticanus has eight, Codex Alexandrinus (followed by the KJV) eighteen. A word "ten" was probably lost in copying. Some harmonizers suggested he was made co-regent with his father at eight. The Plain follows the Hebrew of Chronicles, as is the site's practice, and notes the variant. The "ten days" of his reign are found only here.

a: Zedekiah, his brother
p: Kings says Zedekiah was Jehoiachin's uncle. Here the Hebrew says 'brother', meaning 'relative'.
b: Zedekiah was a son of Josiah (2 Kings 24:17; Jeremiah 1:3), so Jehoiachin's uncle. The Hebrew 'ach can mean any male relative (compare Genesis 14:14, where Lot is Abram's "brother"). The Greek reads "his father's brother," agreeing with Kings. 1 Chronicles 3:16 reads "the sons of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son." Some take this Zedekiah as a second son of Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin's brother, which would support "brother" here; others, following the "his son" chain of 1 Chronicles 3:10–14, take him as Jeconiah's son. See the variant.

a: Before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke for the LORD, he would not humble himself
p: Chronicles judges Zedekiah by his response to Jeremiah, the same test it applied to every king.
b: The book of Jeremiah tells how Zedekiah consulted Jeremiah secretly, kept him in custody and yet would not do what he said (Jeremiah 37:16–21; Jeremiah 38:14–28). Chronicles uses its key word: he did not "humble himself," unlike Manasseh (33:12) and Josiah (34:27). Kings tells Zedekiah's end in detail, his flight, capture and blinding (2 Kings 25:4–7); Chronicles omits it all.

a: though Nebuchadnezzar had put him under oath by God
p: Zedekiah broke an oath sworn in God's name. Ezekiel says this sealed his fate.
b: Ezekiel 17:11–21 tells a parable of two eagles and explains that Zedekiah, having sworn loyalty to Babylon, turned to Egypt: "Will he break the covenant and yet escape?" A vassal oath was sworn by the gods of both parties, so breaking it was a sin against the LORD himself. Chronicles takes Ezekiel's view. It is unusual in the Bible to treat loyalty to a foreign empire as a religious duty, but Jeremiah too urged submission (Jeremiah 27:12).

a: All the leaders of the priests and the people, too, added unfaithfulness to unfaithfulness
p: Kings blames Manasseh for the exile. Chronicles blames the last generation itself: king, priests and people.
b: 2 Kings 24:3–4 says Judah fell "for Manasseh's sins, everything he did," and for the innocent blood he shed. Chronicles, having let Manasseh repent, places the blame on Zedekiah's generation: the leaders polluted the temple and mocked the prophets. This fits Ezekiel's teaching that each generation answers for its own sin (Ezekiel 18:2–4), and Chronicles' pattern across the book. Ezekiel 8 describes what this defilement looked like in the temple in these years.

a: sending early and sending often
p: The Hebrew 'rising early and sending' is a phrase from Jeremiah, where God sends prophet after prophet.
b: Hashkem veshaloach means doing something early and again and again. Jeremiah uses it over and over: "I sent to you all my servants the prophets, rising early and sending them" (Jeremiah 7:25; Jeremiah 25:4; Jeremiah 35:15). Chronicles borrows the phrase to sum up the whole period. It adds a reason: God "felt pity" (chamal) for his people and his dwelling.

a: They, though, made fun of God's messengers
p: Jesus' parable of the vineyard tenants tells the same story: servant after servant sent, all rejected.
b: In Mark 12:1–9 and its parallels, the owner sends servants who are beaten and killed, then his son. Jesus' lament over Jerusalem also echoes this verse: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, killer of the prophets, stoner of those sent to her!" (Matthew 23:37). In Luke 11:50–51 Jesus speaks of the blood of all the prophets "from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah," probably the Zechariah of 2 Chronicles 24:20–22, which suggests Chronicles already stood last in the Bible Jesus used.

a: In their holy house that king put their young men to the sword
p: The temple, a place of refuge, became a place of slaughter.
b: Lamentations asks, "Should a priest and a prophet be put to death inside the Lord's sanctuary?" (Lamentations 2:20). Ezekiel's vision has the slaughter of Jerusalem begin "at my sanctuary" (Ezekiel 9:6). Chronicles does not mention that Nebuzaradan brought the chief priests to Riblah, where the king of Babylon had them put to death (2 Kings 25:18–21). The list "young man or young woman, old man or bent with age" sums up a total disaster, in language like Deuteronomy 32:25.

a: They set God's house on fire and tore down Jerusalem's wall
p: Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC. Excavations show burned houses and arrowheads from the destruction.
b: 2 Kings 25:8–10 dates the burning to the seventh (Jeremiah 52:12: tenth) day of the fifth month in Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year. Excavations in the City of David found a thick burn layer, collapsed houses, Babylonian-type arrowheads, and clay seal impressions baked hard by the fire, including names known from Jeremiah. The "burnt room" and "house of Ahiel" date to this event. Jewish tradition mourns it on the Ninth of Av.

a: Those who escaped the sword he took into exile in Babylon
p: Chronicles implies all survivors went to Babylon. Kings and Jeremiah say the poor were left to farm.
b: 2 Kings 25:12, 22 and Jeremiah 40–41 tell of a community under Gedaliah at Mizpah after the fall. Chronicles leaves them out, giving the picture of a land empty for seventy years, keeping its Sabbaths. Hans Barstad called this "the myth of the empty land," arguing that most of Judah's people stayed; archaeology shows that towns in Benjamin went on with little break. Other historians stress the heavy losses that surveys also show in Judah. Chronicles' picture is theological: the land rests, and the true continuity runs through the exiles who return.

a: This was to fulfill the LORD's word by Jeremiah's mouth
p: The verse joins Jeremiah's seventy years to Leviticus' warning that the land would make up its Sabbaths.
b: Jeremiah wrote, "All this land will become a ruin and a horror, and these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years" (Jeremiah 25:11), and later, "When seventy years for Babylon are over, I will turn my attention to you" (Jeremiah 29:10). Leviticus warned that in exile "the land will make up for its Sabbaths, all the days it lies desolate" (Leviticus 26:34). Chronicles reads the two together: seventy years of rest repay seventy missed sabbatical years, a reading Daniel and later Jewish chronology also assume (Daniel 9:2, 24). The Plain uses the site's wording of Leviticus here; the Jeremiah quotations are translated fresh, since Jeremiah is not yet on the site.
r: Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10; Leviticus 25:1–7; Leviticus 26:34–35; Leviticus 26:43; Daniel 9:2

a: to fill up seventy years
p: From what to what? Several counts have been proposed, and some read seventy as a round number.
b: From 605 BC, when Babylon took control of Judah (Daniel 1:1), to Cyrus' decree in 538 BC is about 67 years. From 586 BC, the temple's fall, to its rebuilding in 516 BC is 70 years, a count Zechariah seems to use (Zechariah 1:12; Zechariah 7:5). Many scholars read seventy as a lifetime, a full span of judgment (Psalm 90:10; Isaiah 23:15), and note an inscription of Esarhaddon: Marduk wrote seventy years as the time of Babylon's desolation, then turned the tablet over to make it eleven. The Talmud counts the years and has Belshazzar and Ahasuerus each miscount them (Bavli Megillah 11b–12a). Traditional Christian reckoning often runs from 605 to 536 or 538 BC. Daniel 9 rereads the seventy as seventy weeks of years; see the topic on Daniel.
r: Jeremiah 25:11–12; Zechariah 1:12; Zechariah 7:5; Daniel 9:2; Daniel 9:24; Psalm 90:10; Isaiah 23:15

a: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia
p: Cyrus II of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC. His first year as its king was 538 BC.
b: Cyrus founded the Persian empire and took Babylon almost without a fight in October 539 BC. The Cyrus Cylinder, found at Babylon in 1879 and now in the British Museum, has him claim that Marduk chose him, that he let deported peoples return to their homes, and that he restored their gods' shrines. It does not mention Judah, and it speaks of Mesopotamian sites, but it shows a policy like the one Ezra describes. Isaiah calls Cyrus the LORD's "anointed" and "shepherd" (Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1).
r: Ezra 1:1–4; Ezra 6:3–5; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1–4; Daniel 1:21; Daniel 6:28

a: the LORD roused the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia
p: The same phrase is used when God stirs up foreign kings to punish or to restore.
b: God "roused the spirit" of the Philistines and Arabs against Jehoram (21:16) and of Pul king of Assyria against the eastern tribes (1 Chronicles 5:26). Now he rouses a foreign king to send his people home. The verb he'ir is used of Cyrus in Isaiah 41:2, 41:25 and 45:13. Chronicles' last chapter thus ends where its exile began, with God at work through emperors.
orig: הֵעִיר יְהוָה אֶת־רוּחַ כּוֹרֶשׁ (he'ir YHWH et-ruach Koresh)
r: 2 Chronicles 21:16; 1 Chronicles 5:26; Isaiah 41:2; Isaiah 41:25; Isaiah 45:13; Haggai 1:14

a: He sent a proclamation through his whole kingdom, and in writing as well
p: 36:22–23 is repeated almost word for word as the opening of Ezra (Ezra 1:1–3).
b: Ezra 1:1–3 repeats these verses and continues the decree: "let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD." Ezra 1:1 reads "from the mouth of Jeremiah" (mippi), where Chronicles has "by the mouth" (befi). Older scholars took the overlap as proof that one author wrote Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah; Sara Japhet and Hugh Williamson argued they are separate works and that these verses were added to Chronicles to link them. 1 Esdras runs straight on from Chronicles into Ezra (1 Esdras 2:1–5), and its 2:1 agrees with Chronicles' "by the mouth." The Plain translates these verses fresh; Ezra is not yet on the site.

a: the LORD, the God of the heavens
p: 'God of the heavens' is a title common in the Persian period, used by Persian officials and by Jews speaking to them.
b: The phrase is rare in older books but frequent in Ezra, Nehemiah and Daniel (Ezra 1:2; Ezra 5:11–12; Nehemiah 1:4; Daniel 2:18). It is also used in the Elephantine papyri of the Jewish colony in Egypt about 410 BC. Persian kings honored local gods in their own terms, as the Cyrus Cylinder does Marduk; a Jewish version of Cyrus' decree naturally names the LORD.
r: Ezra 1:2; Ezra 5:11–12; Ezra 6:9–10; Nehemiah 1:4; Daniel 2:18; Jonah 1:9

a: let him go up
t: The last word of the Hebrew Bible
p: In the Jewish order, Chronicles ends the Bible. Its last word is 'let him go up', an open invitation.
b: In most Hebrew Bibles Chronicles stands last, and the Bible ends with veya'al, "and let him go up," a word later used for moving to the land of Israel (aliyah). The great medieval codices of Aleppo and Leningrad put it first among the Writings. The Christian Old Testament, following the Greek order, places Chronicles among the histories and ends with the prophets, so Malachi's promise of Elijah leads into the Gospels. Jewish readers have heard in the ending a call to return; Christian readers note that Jesus' words in Luke 11:51 may assume Chronicles closed the canon.
